readings.title: Origin of Species: Do domestic breeds revert? (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Identify the objection Darwin answers and the kind of evidence he says would settle it.
readings.focus: Whether domestic breeds can count as evidence about species in nature.
readings.context: Chapter I argues from tame animals and cultivated plants toward wild species. Darwin has just admitted that the laws of inheritance are unknown. Reversion is a return to an ancestral form; the aboriginal stock is the original wild ancestor; esculent means edible; a difference of “generic value” is large enough to separate genera.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication,” from the claim that domestic varieties revert when run wild to the question of single or several parent-species; opens “Having alluded to the subject of reversion, I may here refer to a statement often made by…”; closes “…domestic races, there is presumptive, or even strong, evidence in favour of this view.”.

questions.prompt: What objection does the first paragraph answer, and why would it damage Darwin’s whole argument if it were true?
facilitatorNotes: Naturalists claim that domestic varieties revert to the wild stock when run wild, so nothing can be inferred from domestic races to natural species. Darwin’s method depends on that inference, so he asks for the “decisive facts” behind the claim and lists the difficulties of proving it.
evidence: Hence it has been argued that no deductions can be drawn from domestic races to species in a state of nature.
I have in vain endeavoured to discover on what decisive facts

questions.prompt: Darwin imagines an experiment on cabbages in poor soil, then says its result “is not of great importance.” Why?
facilitatorNotes: Turning a breed loose changes its conditions of life, so reversion there would not show a tendency to revert under unchanged conditions. That is the claim that matters, and for it there is “not a shadow of evidence”: breeders have kept horses, cattle and vegetables true for generations.
evidence: for by the experiment itself the conditions of life are changed
But there is not a shadow of evidence in favour of this view

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin treat the disagreements of “competent judges” as evidence?
facilitatorNotes: Almost every domestic race has been called a variety by some judges and a descendant of a distinct species by others. Such constant doubt suggests there is no sharp line between races and species. Readers can ask whether the disagreement shows that the categories blend or only that the judges lack information.
evidence: If any marked distinction existed between domestic races and species, this source of doubt could not so perpetually recur.

questions.prompt: What would follow if all the dog breeds named here came from one wild species, and why does Darwin decline that convenient conclusion?
facilitatorNotes: It would shake belief in the fixity of closely allied wild species such as the foxes. But Darwin says he does not believe all dogs come from one species, and claims only “presumptive, or even strong” evidence for single origin in some other races. He gives up an example that would suit him.
evidence: then such facts would have great weight in making us doubt about the immutability
I do not believe, as we shall presently see, that all our dogs have descended from any one wild species

readings.title: Origin of Species: One wild ancestor or many? (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow how Darwin accepts part of a rival view while rejecting its extreme form.
readings.focus: Deep time, geography and the limits of crossing as explanations of domestic breeds.
readings.context: Recap: Darwin has answered the claim that domestic breeds revert to wild stock and argued that breeds differ in the way allied species do; he doubts that all dogs come from one wild species. Here he weighs single against multiple origins. Mr. Horner, Mr. Blyth and Sir John Sebright were researchers and breeders of his day; Canidæ is the dog family; a mongrel is a cross between breeds.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference. He uses “savage” and “barbarian” for peoples he ranked below Europeans, a period hierarchy to examine rather than accept.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication,” from the supposed choice of variable animals for taming to the failure of crossing to make new races; opens “It has often been assumed that man has chosen for domestication animals and plants having…”; closes “…nor can I find a single case on record of a permanent race having been thus formed.”.

questions.prompt: How does Darwin answer the assumption that early people chose to tame animals with a special tendency to vary?
facilitatorNotes: The first tamer could not have foreseen variability or hardiness, and animals that vary little or suit only one climate, such as the ass and the camel, were tamed anyway. Darwin predicts that any species bred as long would vary as much.
evidence: how could a savage possibly know, when he first tamed an animal, whether it would vary
they would vary on an average as largely

questions.prompt: What does Darwin conclude from the breeds pictured on ancient Egyptian monuments, and why does the evidence of pottery matter?
facilitatorNotes: Diverse breeds in Egypt prove only that some breeds are four or five thousand years old. Pottery from thirteen or fourteen thousand years ago, and people with half-tame dogs before that, push domestication back into time long enough for breeds to form.
evidence: what does it show, but that some of our breeds originated there, four or five thousand years ago?

questions.prompt: Darwin accepts several wild ancestors for dogs but calls the many-ancestors view an “absurd extreme” when pushed. What reasoning draws the line?
facilitatorNotes: Geography: Britain has hardly one mammal of its own, yet one author gives it eleven peculiar wild sheep; each European country has its own breeds but not its own wild species. And no wild canid resembles the bull-dog or Italian greyhound. Breeds must have formed under domestication.
evidence: One author believes that there formerly existed in Great Britain eleven wild species of sheep peculiar to it!
so unlike all wild Canidæ

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin doubt that crossing a few wild species explains the variety of breeds?
facilitatorNotes: Crossing gives only intermediates, so the extreme forms would have had to exist in the wild. A first cross may be uniform, but its descendants scatter until “hardly two of them will be alike,” and Sebright’s experiment failed. This clears the way for selection as the main cause.
evidence: by crossing we can get only forms in some degree intermediate between their parents
nor can I find a single case on record of a permanent race having been thus formed

readings.title: Origin of Species: Why breeders doubt common descent (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Weigh a list of reasons, then notice how Darwin turns experts’ certainty into a warning.
readings.focus: Historical testimony, personal doubt and the blind spot of specialists.
readings.context: Darwin has argued that every breed of domestic pigeon, however different, descends from one wild species, the rock-pigeon (Columba livia). These paragraphs finish the case. Carriers, tumblers and fantails are fancy breeds; a fancier breeds animals for show; Akber Khan is the Mughal emperor Akbar.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication,” the last two paragraphs on the origin of domestic pigeons; opens “In favour of this view, I may add, firstly, that C. livia, or the rock-pigeon, has been…”; closes “…the idea of species in a state of nature being lineal descendants of other species?”.

questions.prompt: Darwin adds four reasons for the rock-pigeon view. Which seems strongest to you, and which depend on chapters still to come?
facilitatorNotes: The rock-pigeon can be tamed and resembles the breeds; sub-breeds form an almost perfect series between extremes; each breed’s distinctive traits are highly variable; and pigeons have been bred with care for thousands of years. The series is the most direct evidence; the third and fourth explicitly point forward to the discussion of selection.
evidence: we can make an almost perfect series between the extremes of structure
the explanation of this fact will be obvious when we come to treat of selection

questions.prompt: Why bring Pliny’s Romans, Akbar’s court and the Dutch into an argument about pigeons?
facilitatorNotes: They show long, intense, worldwide attention to breeding, the conditions under which great variation could accumulate. Historical testimony stands in for the measurements no one made.
evidence: they can reckon up their pedigree and race
His Majesty by crossing the breeds, which method was never practised before, has improved them astonishingly.

questions.prompt: Darwin admits he once found common descent as hard to believe as any naturalist would. Why is that admission useful to his argument?
facilitatorNotes: He meets the reader’s disbelief by sharing it, then shows what changed his mind: keeping and watching pigeons. A converted sceptic is a persuasive witness.
evidence: I felt fully as much difficulty in believing that they could ever have descended from a common parent

questions.prompt: Why are expert breeders convinced that each breed has its own wild ancestor, and what “lesson of caution” does Darwin draw for naturalists?
facilitatorNotes: Long study fixes their eyes on differences; they win prizes by selecting slight variations yet “refuse to sum up” what generations of them could do. Naturalists who accept common descent for breeds against the breeders, but deride it for wild species, may be making the breeders’ mistake.
evidence: refuse to sum up in their minds slight differences accumulated during many successive generations
may they not learn a lesson of caution

readings.title: Origin of Species: Selection without intending it (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Separate the evidence that shows selection from the evidence that shows only attention to breeding.
readings.focus: Unconscious selection: change that no breeder intended.
readings.context: Darwin has shown what breeders achieve by methodical selection, choosing animals to breed toward a goal. Here he answers the objection that selection is a modern practice and names a second kind. Bakewell and Collins were eighteenth-century English stock-breeders; Youatt wrote standard works on livestock; “roguing” is pulling inferior plants from a crop.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference. He uses “savage” and “barbarian” for peoples he ranked below Europeans, a period hierarchy to examine rather than accept. He repeats a travellers’ report, now considered unreliable, that the people of Tierra del Fuego killed old women in famine.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication,” from the antiquity of selection to unconscious selection among peoples who keep animals; opens “It may be objected that the principle of selection has been reduced to methodical…”; closes “…and devouring their old women, in times of dearth, as of less value than their dogs.”.

questions.prompt: How does Darwin show that selection is not a modern discovery, and what does he admit about some of his examples?
facilitatorNotes: He cites English laws on choice animals, a Chinese encyclopaedia, Roman writers, Genesis, Pliny and Livingstone: selection appears across ages and cultures because inheritance is “so obvious.” He concedes that some facts show only careful attention to breeding, not selection.
evidence: Some of these facts do not show actual selection
for the inheritance of good and bad qualities is so obvious

questions.prompt: What is “Unconscious” selection, and why does Darwin call it more important for his purpose than methodical selection?
facilitatorNotes: Breeding from one’s best animals with no wish to change the breed still changes it over centuries. It shows that lasting change needs no plan, which is the bridge from human selection to selection in nature.
evidence: results from every one trying to possess and breed from the best individual animals
he has no wish or expectation of permanently altering the breed

questions.prompt: Why are such slow changes hard to prove, and which of Darwin’s substitute evidence is most convincing?
facilitatorNotes: Without old measurements or drawings, change goes unnoticed. He uses less-improved breeds in remote districts, old pigeon treatises, racehorses that outrun their Arab ancestors, and Youatt’s two Leicester flocks, bred from one stock without intent yet now looking like different varieties. The flocks come closest to a controlled comparison.
evidence: Slow and insensible changes of this kind could never be recognised unless actual measurements or careful drawings
they have the appearance of being quite different varieties

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph, what is Darwin’s argument, and what in its evidence should a reader question?
facilitatorNotes: The logical point is sound: people who never think about inheritance still save their most useful animals in hard times, so selection happens anyway. The supporting example is hearsay wrapped in a ranking of peoples; the argument does not need it, and readers should examine it as prejudice and weak evidence.
evidence: so that in this case there would be a kind of unconscious selection going on
We see the value set on animals even by the barbarians of Tierra del Fuego

readings.title: Origin of Species: Breeds without birthdays (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow how one principle explains several puzzling facts at once.
readings.focus: Why the origins of breeds, like those of dialects, go unrecorded.
readings.context: Recap: Darwin has argued that besides deliberate breeding there is unconscious selection, the habit of breeding from one’s best animals, which slowly changes breeds no one meant to change. Here he applies it to garden plants and to the oddities of breeds. Heartsease is the pansy; a pelargonium is a geranium; the fantail and pouter are pigeon breeds; a bird’s crop is a pouch in its throat.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference. Darwin ranks peoples as “civilised” and “uncivilised,” a period hierarchy, and uses it to explain why no crop plants had come from Australia or the Cape.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication,” from improvement in garden plants to the unrecorded origins of domestic breeds; opens “In plants the same gradual process of improvement, through the occasional preservation of…”; closes “…small of any record having been preserved of such slow, varying, and insensible changes.”.

questions.prompt: Gardeners are praised for “wonderful skill.” Why does Darwin deny that skill was the main cause?
facilitatorNotes: The art was simple: always grow the best known variety, sow its seed, and keep any slightly better seedling. The result built up almost unconsciously; the classical gardeners never imagined our pears.
evidence: the art, I cannot doubt, has been simple
never thought what splendid fruit we should eat

questions.prompt: Darwin says no region “inhabited by quite uncivilised man” has given Europe a plant worth growing. What does this claim assume, and how could it be tested?
facilitatorNotes: It assumes that worth means worth to European gardens and that such peoples selected nothing. A test would need evidence of what those peoples grew and how; Darwin offers none, so the claim rests on his ranking of peoples.
evidence: neither Australia, the Cape of Good Hope, nor any other region inhabited by quite uncivilised man, has afforded us a single plant worth culture

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin call the phrase “trying to make a fantail” “utterly incorrect”?
facilitatorNotes: A breeder can only select variations that nature first supplies; the man who kept a pigeon with a slightly larger tail never imagined the fantail. The breed is an accumulation, not a design, the key step toward natural selection.
evidence: He can never act by selection, excepting on variations which are first given to him in some slight degree by nature.
never dreamed what the descendants of that pigeon would become

questions.prompt: What does comparing a breed to “a dialect of a language” explain?
facilitatorNotes: A breed has no definite birth: improved animals spread locally, get a provincial name only when valued, and leave no record of their slow beginnings. So our ignorance of breed origins is what the theory predicts, not evidence against it. Readers may extend the analogy to species.
evidence: a breed, like a dialect of a language, can hardly be said to have had a definite origin
the chance will be infinitely small of any record having been preserved

readings.title: Origin of Species: What favours the breeder, and the chapter’s verdict (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Track the hedges in a summary, then weigh the confident claim that closes it.
readings.focus: The conditions that let selection work, and selection named as the predominant cause.
readings.context: Recap: Darwin has argued that gardeners and fanciers improve plants and animals by selecting slight variations, mostly without a plan, and that breeds, like dialects, have no recorded beginnings. Now he lists what makes selection succeed or fail, then sums up the chapter. William Marshall wrote on English farming; correlation of growth means that changing one part changes others with it.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication,” from the circumstances favourable to selection to the end of the chapter; opens “I must now say a few words on the circumstances, favourable, or the reverse, to man’s…”; closes “…or unconsciously and more slowly, but more efficiently, is by far the predominant Power.”.

questions.prompt: Why does a large number of individuals matter so much to selection?
facilitatorNotes: Useful variations are rare, so more individuals give more chances; when stock is scarce every animal is bred and selection stops. Hence Marshall’s poor Yorkshire flocks “never can be improved,” while nurserymen outdo amateurs.
evidence: the chance of their appearance will be much increased by a large number of individuals being kept
they never can be improved

questions.prompt: What does the strawberry example show about variation and attention?
facilitatorNotes: The strawberry “had always varied”; new varieties seemed to appear only when gardeners began picking out the best plants, because attention let selection accumulate the differences. Darwin mocks the remark that reverses cause and effect.
evidence: I have seen it gravely remarked, that it was most fortunate that the strawberry began to vary just when gardeners began to attend closely to this plant.
No doubt the strawberry had always varied

questions.prompt: How does Darwin explain why cats, donkeys, peacocks and geese have few distinct breeds?
facilitatorNotes: Not by a lack of variation but by selection never being applied: cats cannot be paired, donkeys are kept in small numbers by the poor, peacocks are hard to rear, and geese are valued only for food and feathers. The theory explains an absence as well as a presence.
evidence: may be attributed in main part to selection not having been brought into play

questions.prompt: The summary lists many causes of variation, then names one “predominant Power.” How much does Darwin claim, and how much does he admit not knowing?
facilitatorNotes: He names conditions of life, inheritance and reversion, unknown laws, correlation, use and disuse, and crossing, and calls the result “infinitely complex.” After these hedges comes a confident verdict for selection. Readers can judge whether the chapter has earned the capital P.
evidence: The final result is thus rendered infinitely complex.
is by far the predominant Power

readings.title: Origin of Species: Species or variety? The experts disagree (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Use disagreement among experts as evidence about the categories they use.
readings.focus: Why naturalists cannot agree where varieties end and species begin.
readings.context: Chapter II asks whether wild species vary as domestic breeds do. Darwin has just said that naturalists have no agreed definition of a species. A flora is a catalogue of a region’s plants; polymorphic means occurring in many forms; the primrose and cowslip are related wildflowers; Gärtner was a German expert on plant crossing.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Variation under Nature,” from the frequency of doubtful forms to the young naturalist’s difficulties; opens “That varieties of this doubtful nature are far from uncommon cannot be disputed. Compare…”; closes “…have to trust almost entirely to analogy, and his difficulties will rise to a climax.”.

questions.prompt: What does the gap between Babington’s 251 species and Bentham’s 112 show?
facilitatorNotes: Two botanists describe the same British plants and differ by 139 “doubtful forms”: rank depends on the judge. The exclamation mark shows how striking Darwin finds it.
evidence: a difference of 139 doubtful forms!

questions.prompt: How does distance affect the ranking of doubtful forms, and why does Darwin ask what distance “will suffice”?
facilitatorNotes: Naturalists tend to call separated forms distinct species, but no distance can be named as the threshold: America and Europe, the Azores, Madeira, Ireland. The question exposes how arbitrary the line is, as Darwin felt with the Galápagos birds.
evidence: what distance, it has been well asked, will suffice?
how entirely vague and arbitrary is the distinction between species and varieties

questions.prompt: What evidence suggests that the primrose and cowslip are separate species, and what leads Darwin to call them varieties?
facilitatorNotes: They differ in look, flavour, smell, flowering time, station, altitude and range, and cross only with difficulty: “hardly” better evidence could be wished for. But intermediate links that are probably not hybrids, and much experiment, show common parents. He states the strongest case for distinctness before overturning it.
evidence: We could hardly wish for better evidence of the two forms being specifically distinct.
they descend from common parents, and consequently must be ranked as varieties

questions.prompt: How does the young naturalist’s judgment change as he studies more widely, and what does that suggest about the categories?
facilitatorNotes: At first he multiplies species, impressed by differences like the pigeon-fancier; wider study brings more hard cases; he settles them only by admitting much variation, and with forms from distant countries he must rely on analogy. The categories reflect the observer’s range of knowledge as much as nature.
evidence: His general tendency will be to make many species
he will have to trust almost entirely to analogy, and his difficulties will rise to a climax

readings.title: Origin of Species: Varieties as species in the making (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Distinguish what Darwin infers from a series of forms from what he says remains to be proved.
readings.focus: Species as named stages in a continuous process, and a prediction that can be tested.
readings.context: Recap: Darwin has shown that competent naturalists constantly disagree whether a form is a species or a variety, as with the primrose and cowslip. Now he draws his conclusion and proposes a test. Incipient means beginning; a genus (plural genera) is a group of closely related species; Alphonse de Candolle and Joseph Hooker were leading botanists.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Variation under Nature,” from the lack of any clear line between species and varieties to the prediction about large genera; opens “Certainly no clear line of demarcation has as yet been drawn between species and…”; closes “…why more varieties should occur in a group having many species, than in one having few.”.

questions.prompt: Darwin arranges individual differences, varieties, sub-species and species in one series. What does he infer from it, and how far does he say the inference is proved?
facilitatorNotes: A graded series “impresses the mind with the idea of an actual passage”: a well-marked variety is an incipient species. But a series of forms does not by itself prove movement along it, and Darwin says the belief must be judged by the weight of the whole book.
evidence: a series impresses the mind with the idea of an actual passage
a well-marked variety may be justly called an incipient species

questions.prompt: What does Darwin mean by calling “species” a term “arbitrarily given for the sake of convenience”?
facilitatorNotes: Species and variety differ in degree, and the names mark convenient points on a continuum rather than fixed natural kinds. In 1859, when species were widely held to be separately created and fixed, this was a radical claim. Readers may ask whether a name can be arbitrary while the groups it names are real.
evidence: I look at the term species, as one arbitrarily given for the sake of convenience

questions.prompt: Why should the dominant species of a country produce the most varieties?
facilitatorNotes: Widely spread, common species meet more conditions and competitors, and their slightly modified offspring inherit the advantages that made the parents dominant, so their varieties are likelier to last. Darwin notes that Hooker checked the tables, while saying the subject is “rather perplexing.”
evidence: which oftenest produce well-marked varieties, or, as I consider them, incipient species
will still inherit those advantages that enabled their parents to become dominant

questions.prompt: Darwin predicts that species in large genera should vary more. Why does his view predict this, while independent creation gives “no apparent reason” for it?
facilitatorNotes: Where many species have formed, conditions have favoured variation and probably still do: where there are large trees, expect saplings. Separate creation predicts nothing about the pattern. A theory that risks a testable prediction is stronger than one that can accommodate any result.
evidence: Where many large trees grow, we expect to find saplings.
there is no apparent reason why more varieties should occur in a group having many species

readings.title: Origin of Species: The manufactory of species (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Evaluate a numerical test and the limits Darwin places on what it shows.
readings.focus: A predicted pattern in the catalogues, and the argument that only descent explains it.
readings.context: Recap: Darwin has argued that varieties are species in the making and predicted that species in large genera, where many species have already formed, should now produce more varieties. Here he reports his test and sums up the chapter. Coleopterous insects are beetles; Fries and Westwood were naturalists; Watson divided Great Britain into botanical provinces.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Variation under Nature,” from the test of the large-genera prediction to the end of the chapter; opens “To test the truth of this anticipation I have arranged the plants of twelve countries,…”; closes “…forms of life throughout the universe become divided into groups subordinate to groups.”.

questions.prompt: How did Darwin test his prediction, and what did he do to guard against a misleading result?
facilitatorNotes: He split the plants of twelve countries and the beetles of two districts into larger and smaller genera, and found more varying species, and more varieties per species, in the larger genera. He repeated the division with the smallest genera excluded and got the same result.
evidence: it has invariably proved to be the case
when all the smallest genera, with from only one to four species, are absolutely excluded from the tables

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin say that a perfect result, every large genus varying and no small one, “would have been fatal” to his theory?
facilitatorNotes: Geology shows small genera growing and large ones declining and vanishing, so the theory predicts only an average tendency. An absolute pattern would contradict the fossil record. The claim is deliberately limited.
evidence: for if this had been so, it would have been fatal to my theory
All that we want to show is, that where many species of a genus have been formed, on an average many are still forming

questions.prompt: What does the “manufactory of species” metaphor contribute, and how might it mislead?
facilitatorNotes: It makes species-formation an ongoing, slow process: where the factory has been busy it is still running. But a factory implies a maker and a plan, which Darwin’s argument denies; his “if we may use the expression” shows he knows it.
evidence: the manufactory of species has been active
if we may use the expression

questions.prompt: The chapter ends by calling these analogies “utterly inexplicable” if each species was independently created. How strong is that kind of argument?
facilitatorNotes: It argues to the best explanation: clustering “like satellites,” small differences and restricted ranges all fit species that began as varieties. Independent creation could be stretched to allow any pattern, but it explains none of them. Readers can say what evidence would weaken Darwin’s case.
evidence: little groups of species are generally clustered like satellites around certain other species
these analogies are utterly inexplicable if each species has been independently created

readings.title: Origin of Species: What keeps numbers down? (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Sort Darwin’s checks on increase by kind, and notice where he admits he does not know.
readings.focus: Food, enemies, climate and disease as checks on numbers, and why climate mostly acts through other species.
readings.context: Darwin has argued that every species tends to multiply far faster than its food and space allow, so that many more are born than can survive: the struggle for existence. Here he asks what actually keeps numbers down. Vermin here means animals that prey on game, such as foxes, stoats and hawks; game is animals hunted for sport; rape-seed is an oil crop; a naturalised plant spreads by itself in a new country.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence,” from the obscurity of the checks to the need for a large stock; opens “What checks the natural tendency of each species to increase in number is most obscure.…”; closes “…into play in some of these cases; but on this intricate subject I will not here enlarge.”.

questions.prompt: Darwin opens, “What checks the natural tendency of each species to increase in number is most obscure.” How does he handle his own ignorance in the first paragraph?
facilitatorNotes: He admits “We know not exactly what the checks are in even one single instance,” compares our ignorance about mankind, promises a fuller treatment later, and offers only “a few remarks.” Admitting the limits of knowledge makes the observations that follow more credible, not less.
evidence: We know not exactly what the checks are in even one single instance.

questions.prompt: What did Darwin do on his plot of cleared ground, and what did it show? What does the plot of turf add?
facilitatorNotes: He marked every seedling of native weeds on a cleared patch three feet by two: of 357, 295 were destroyed, chiefly by slugs and insects, with no other plants to choke them. Left to grow, a plot of turf lost nine of its twenty species to more vigorous ones. Two small, counted observations show destruction by enemies and by competitors separately.
evidence: out of the 357 no less than 295 were destroyed, chiefly by slugs and insects
nine species perished from the other species being allowed to grow up freely

questions.prompt: Darwin predicts that if no game were shot and no vermin destroyed for twenty years, there would be less game in England. Why is this surprising, and what principle does it illustrate?
facilitatorNotes: One expects game to multiply if no one hunts it. But predators kill more than hunters, so “serving as prey,” not food, sets the average numbers. The thought experiment separates two causes that ordinary experience confuses.
evidence: it is not the obtaining food, but the serving as prey to other animals, which determines the average numbers of a species
there would, in all probability, be less game than at present

questions.prompt: When a species grows rarer toward the north, why does Darwin call it “a very false view” to blame the climate alone?
facilitatorNotes: Climate mostly acts indirectly, by reducing food or by favouring the species’ enemies and competitors; garden plants that can bear the English climate still never run wild, because they cannot compete. Only at the extremes, the Arctic or the desert, is the struggle “almost exclusively with the elements.” Students can test the claim with the garden example.
evidence: But this is a very false view
they cannot compete with our native plants, nor resist destruction by our native animals

readings.title: Origin of Species: The entangled bank and the nearest rivals (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow Darwin from a picture of complex causes to a claim about who competes hardest.
readings.focus: Why the mix of plants on a bank is not chance, and why the struggle is fiercest between close relatives.
readings.context: Darwin has listed the checks that keep each species from multiplying without limit: food, enemies, climate and disease. Here he looks at how many checks combine and who competes with whom. The “Indian mounds” are earthworks built centuries earlier by Native American peoples in the Mississippi and Ohio valleys; a congener is a species of the same genus; the missel-thrush is the mistle thrush; charlock is a weedy wild mustard.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference. Darwin calls Native American earthworks “Indian mounds” and “old Indian ruins,” period terms.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence,” from the many checks on every species to the competition of allied species; opens “In the case of every species, many different checks, acting at different periods of life,…”; closes “…say why one species has been victorious over another in the great battle of life.”.

questions.prompt: Darwin warns against attributing the mix of plants on “an entangled bank” to chance. What evidence does he give from the trees on the old mounds?
facilitatorNotes: Trees growing on the ancient mounds show “the same beautiful diversity and proportion of kinds” as the virgin forest around them. If chance ruled, the mounds should differ; the same result reached independently points to definite causes working over centuries. A cut forest, by contrast, grows back different, because its conditions have changed.
evidence: we are tempted to attribute their proportional numbers and kinds to what we call chance. But how false a view is this!
display the same beautiful diversity and proportion of kinds as in the surrounding virgin forests

questions.prompt: What is the comparison with a handful of feathers claiming?
facilitatorNotes: Feathers fall “according to definite laws,” yet the problem is simple. The plants and animals of a forest are also governed by causes, only far more of them, acting and reacting for centuries. What we call chance is a name for causes too many to follow.
evidence: Throw up a handful of feathers, and all must fall to the ground according to definite laws

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin think the struggle is “most severe between the individuals of the same species”? What do the wheat and sweet-peas show?
facilitatorNotes: They share districts, food and dangers. Mixed varieties of wheat sown together end with the best-suited varieties supplanting the rest, and coloured sweet-peas must be harvested separately each year or “the weaker kinds will steadily decrease in numbers and disappear.” Farmers’ practice serves as an experiment.
evidence: for they frequent the same districts, require the same food, and are exposed to the same dangers
otherwise the weaker kinds will steadily decrease in numbers and disappear

questions.prompt: What do the swallows, thrushes, rats and cockroaches have in common, and what limit does Darwin admit at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Each is a species replacing a close relative of the same genus, which fills “nearly the same place in the economy of nature.” But he concedes that in no single case could we say exactly why one won. He can show the pattern without knowing the mechanism in any instance.
evidence: One species of charlock will supplant another
probably in no one case could we precisely say why one species has been victorious over another

readings.title: Origin of Species: Every structure answers to its rivals (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Test a general principle against the examples that seem least to fit it.
readings.focus: Darwin’s corollary that each being’s structure is shaped by other beings, and his consoling close.
readings.context: Recap: Darwin has argued that the struggle for existence is fiercest between individuals of the same species and between closely related species, though no one can say exactly why one wins. Here he draws a conclusion and closes Chapter III. A corollary follows from something already shown; the confines of a range are its outer edges; increase at a geometrical ratio multiplies, as 2, 4, 8, 16.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence,” from the corollary on structure to the end of the chapter; opens “A corollary of the highest importance may be deduced from the foregoing remarks, namely,…”; closes “…generally prompt, and that the vigorous, the healthy, and the happy survive and multiply.”.

questions.prompt: State the “corollary of the highest importance” in your own words. Why does Darwin choose the dandelion seed and the water-beetle rather than the tiger’s teeth to illustrate it?
facilitatorNotes: Every organism’s structure is related, often in hidden ways, to the organisms it competes with, escapes or eats. The tiger is obvious; the plumed seed and the diving beetle seem shaped only by air and water. Showing that even these answer to other living things (crowded ground, rival insects, predators) makes the principle stronger.
evidence: the structure of every organic being is related, in the most essential yet often hidden manner, to that of all other organic beings
the relation seems at first confined to the elements of air and water

questions.prompt: How does Darwin reason about the food stored in seeds, and how confident is he?
facilitatorNotes: From peas and beans growing strongly in long grass, he suspects the store is for the seedling “whilst struggling with other plants.” It is an inference from one kind of observation, and “I suspect” marks it as a hypothesis.
evidence: I suspect that the chief use of the nutriment in the seed is to favour the growth of the young seedling

questions.prompt: Darwin asks the reader to imagine giving a plant an advantage. What does this thought experiment teach?
facilitatorNotes: We would have to give it an edge over competitors or enemies, and a different edge in a new country, and “Probably in no single instance should we know what to do.” The exercise is meant to fail: it exposes our ignorance of how living things depend on one another, a conviction Darwin calls necessary and hard to acquire.
evidence: Probably in no single instance should we know what to do, so as to succeed.
a conviction as necessary, as it seems to be difficult to acquire

questions.prompt: The chapter ends with consolation: the war of nature “is not incessant,” “no fear is felt,” “death is generally prompt.” Is this a scientific claim, or something else? Has the chapter earned it?
facilitatorNotes: Part of it follows from the chapter (destruction comes at intervals and seasons); “no fear is felt” is not something Darwin has shown. Readers may see a humane reassurance to Victorian readers troubled by a “war of nature,” or a softening that sits oddly with 295 dead seedlings in 357. Both judgments should rest on the wording.
evidence: we may console ourselves with the full belief, that the war of nature is not incessant
the vigorous, the healthy, and the happy survive and multiply

readings.title: Origin of Species: Small features and every stage of life (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Identify the objection Darwin is answering in each paragraph.
readings.focus: Natural selection acting on colour, on the young, and never for another species’ sake.
readings.context: Darwin has introduced natural selection, the preservation of favourable variations and the destruction of harmful ones in the struggle for existence, and compared it with a breeder’s selection. Here he answers the objection that small features such as colour cannot matter. The ptarmigan and grouse are game birds; a curculio is a weevil; correlation of growth means that a change in one part brings changes in others; tumbler-pigeons are a fancy breed with very short beaks; fanciers are hobby breeders.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Natural Selection,” from characters of trifling importance to the beaks of nestling pigeons; opens “Although natural selection can act only through and for the good of each being, yet…”; closes “…be selected, the thickness of the shell being known to vary like every other structure.”.

questions.prompt: Darwin argues that features “of very trifling importance” can be acted on by natural selection. What is his evidence from grouse and from fruit?
facilitatorNotes: Insects and grouse match their backgrounds, and hawks hunt by sight, so that white pigeons are the first taken. Downing reports that smooth-skinned fruits suffer more from a weevil than downy ones, and that colour affects disease. If such differences matter even in a tended orchard, they would decide survival in the wild.
evidence: hawks are guided by eyesight to their prey
smooth-skinned fruits suffer far more from a beetle, a curculio, than those with down

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin mention that a sheep farmer must destroy “every lamb with the faintest trace of black”?
facilitatorNotes: It answers the objection that occasional deaths of one colour would have little effect. The breeder’s practice shows that steady removal of a trait keeps a flock uniform; predators that take conspicuous birds act the same way.
evidence: Nor ought we to think that the occasional destruction of an animal of any particular colour would produce little effect
how essential it is in a flock of white sheep to destroy every lamb with the faintest trace of black

questions.prompt: What does Darwin say natural selection “cannot do,” and what kind of evidence would prove him wrong?
facilitatorNotes: It cannot modify one species, without any advantage to it, purely for the good of another. He says he has found no claimed case that “will bear investigation.” A single well-established case would refute him, which makes this a testable claim; students can see how a theory states what it forbids.
evidence: What natural selection cannot do, is to modify the structure of one species, without giving it any advantage, for the good of another species
I cannot find one case which will bear investigation

questions.prompt: What problem do short-beaked tumbler-pigeons pose, and what two solutions does Darwin imagine for nature?
facilitatorNotes: The best short-beaked birds often cannot break out of the egg, so fanciers help them hatch. In nature, selection would favour chicks with the hardest beaks inside the egg, or thinner shells. The example shows selection working at every stage of life, even before hatching.
evidence: more perish in the egg than are able to get out of it
more delicate and more easily broken shells might be selected

readings.title: Origin of Species: Sexual selection, and an imaginary wolf (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Distinguish a definition, a reported observation and an imagined illustration.
readings.focus: A second kind of selection, between rivals for mates, and a thought experiment about wolves.
readings.context: Darwin has argued that natural selection can act on small features and at every stage of life. Here he names a second process, sexual selection, then offers “imaginary illustrations.” Polygamous animals are those in which one male mates with many females; bantams are small ornamental chickens; carriers are a pigeon breed and the wattle a fleshy growth on the head; Sir R. Heron, Mr. St. John and Mr. Pierce are observers whose reports Darwin cites.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference. Darwin compares fighting alligators to “Indians in a war-dance,” a period stereotype of Native Americans.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Natural Selection,” the sections on sexual selection and the first illustration of natural selection; opens “_Sexual Selection_.—Inasmuch as peculiarities often appear under domestication in one sex…”; closes “…other more bulky, with shorter legs, which more frequently attacks the shepherd’s flocks.”.

questions.prompt: How does sexual selection differ from natural selection in Darwin’s definition, and why does he call it “less rigorous”?
facilitatorNotes: It is a struggle between males for females, not a struggle for existence, and losing means few or no offspring rather than death. Since the loser lives, the selection is milder, but it still decides which traits are passed on.
evidence: This depends, not on a struggle for existence, but on a struggle between the males for possession of the females
the result is not death to the unsuccessful competitor, but few or no offspring

questions.prompt: Darwin describes two ways males win: battle and attraction. What examples does he give of each, and what part do the females play in the second?
facilitatorNotes: Weapons and shields (horns, spurs, the lion’s mane, the hooked jaw of the salmon) win battles. Among birds, males sing and display, and the females “at last choose the most attractive partner.” Darwin gives females an active role, choosing “according to their standard of beauty,” as a breeder chooses bantams by his.
evidence: for the shield may be as important for victory, as the sword or spear
at last choose the most attractive partner
according to their standard of beauty

questions.prompt: Where does Darwin limit his own explanation, and why does the turkey-cock’s tuft matter to him?
facilitatorNotes: He will not attribute all differences between the sexes to sexual selection: some, like the tuft, seem neither useful in battle nor attractive, and would be called a “monstrosity” in a domestic bird. Naming a case his idea does not explain shows the limits he accepts.
evidence: I would not wish to attribute all such sexual differences to this agency
can hardly be either useful or ornamental to this bird

questions.prompt: Darwin calls the wolf an “imaginary illustration.” What conditions does he set for swift wolves to be selected, and what real report does he add at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Swift prey must become commoner, or other prey scarcer, when food is short, and the slim wolves must keep the strength to master prey at other times. Inherited hunting habits in cats support the idea of innate tendencies, and Mr. Pierce reports two forms of wolf in the Catskills, one greyhound-like that hunts deer. Students can judge how far an imagined case plus a report supports the claim.
evidence: I must beg permission to give one or two imaginary illustrations
provided always that they retained strength to master their prey
there are two varieties of the wolf inhabiting the Catskill Mountains

readings.title: Origin of Species: Why flowers cross (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Find the facts Darwin says are inexplicable on any other view, and judge whether his law explains them.
readings.focus: Darwin’s proposed law that no plant or animal fertilises itself forever.
readings.context: Darwin interrupts his account of natural selection with what he calls “a short digression.” Many plants are hermaphrodites, with male and female parts in the same flower: anthers and stamens carry pollen, and the stigma and pistil receive it. Papilionaceous flowers belong to the pea family; a hybridizer crosses plants on purpose; a camel-hair pencil is a fine brush. Andrew Knight, Gärtner, Kölreuter and C. C. Sprengel were earlier students of plant breeding and pollination.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Natural Selection,” from “On the Intercrossing of Individuals” to the Lobelia; opens “_On the Intercrossing of Individuals_.—I must here introduce a short digression. In the…”; closes “…of an occasional cross with a distinct individual being advantageous or indispensable!”.

questions.prompt: What “general law of nature” does Darwin propose, and what first inclines him to believe it?
facilitatorNotes: That no organism fertilises itself “for an eternity of generations”; an occasional cross with another individual is indispensable. The breeders’ experience that crosses bring vigour and close interbreeding weakness inclines him to it, though he admits he is “utterly ignorant” of the law’s meaning.
evidence: no organic being self-fertilises itself for an eternity of generations
utterly ignorant though we be of the meaning of the law

questions.prompt: Darwin says some facts are inexplicable “on any other view.” Choose one, the exposed flowers or the pea-flowers and bees, and explain how his law accounts for it.
facilitatorNotes: Wet harms fertilisation, yet many flowers leave their organs open to the weather: openness admits pollen from other plants. Pea-flowers are closed, but bees push pollen in as they feed, and when Darwin kept bees away their fertility fell. In both, the structure makes sense if crossing matters.
evidence: what a multitude of flowers have their anthers and stigmas fully exposed to the weather!
their fertility is greatly diminished if these visits be prevented

questions.prompt: If bees carry pollen from flower to flower, why don’t they make “a multitude of hybrids between distinct species”?
facilitatorNotes: A plant’s own pollen is “prepotent” over pollen of another species and wipes out its influence, as Gärtner showed. Darwin anticipates the objection and answers it with another researcher’s experiments.
evidence: it must not be supposed that bees would thus produce a multitude of hybrids between distinct species

questions.prompt: What did Darwin observe and do with Lobelia fulgens, and why does he exclaim “How strange are these facts!”?
facilitatorNotes: Its flowers sweep out their pollen before their own stigma is ready; no insects visit it in his garden, so it sets no seed, yet hand-crossing gave “plenty of seedlings,” while a bee-visited Lobelia nearby seeded freely. Organs placed as if for self-fertilisation are often useless to each other, which his law explains.
evidence: it never sets a seed, though by placing pollen from one flower on the stigma of another, I raised plenty of seedlings
How strange are these facts!

readings.title: Origin of Species: Cabbages, trees and earthworms (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Count how Darwin qualifies a claim while gathering evidence for it.
readings.focus: Experiments, objections and exceptions behind the law of the occasional cross.
readings.context: Recap: Darwin has proposed that no plant or animal fertilises itself forever and that an occasional cross with another individual is necessary; flowers, he argues, are built to take pollen from other flowers, often carried by insects. Mongrels are crosses between varieties; prepotent means stronger in effect; cirripedes are barnacles; Hooker, Asa Gray and Huxley were leading naturalists of the day.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Natural Selection,” from the mongrel cabbages to the end of the section on intercrossing; opens “If several varieties of the cabbage, radish, onion, and of some other plants, be allowed…”; closes “…long intervals; but in none, as I suspect, can self-fertilisation go on for perpetuity.”.

questions.prompt: What did Darwin find when cabbages of different varieties seeded near one another, and why was the result surprising?
facilitatorNotes: Of 233 seedlings only 78 were true to their kind. Each flower’s pistil is surrounded by its own stamens and those of the same plant, so self-fertilisation should have dominated. He suspects that pollen of another variety is prepotent over a flower’s own, the reverse of what happens between species.
evidence: I raised 233 seedling cabbages from some plants of different varieties growing near each other, and of these only 78 were true to their kind
Yet the pistil of each cabbage-flower is surrounded not only by its own six stamens

questions.prompt: What objection about large trees does Darwin raise against himself, and how does he treat the evidence from New Zealand, the United States and Australia?
facilitatorNotes: Pollen may rarely pass from tree to tree, and flowers on one tree are hardly separate individuals; he calls the objection “valid.” He predicts that trees more often have separate sexes, and colleagues’ tables confirm it, but Hooker reports that the rule fails in Australia. He prints the exception and claims only to “call attention to the subject.”
evidence: I believe this objection to be valid
he finds that the rule does not hold in Australia

questions.prompt: Why, on Darwin’s view, do land hermaphrodites such as earthworms always pair, while some water animals fertilise themselves?
facilitatorNotes: On land there is no carrier, like insects or wind for plants, that could bring an occasional cross, so two individuals must meet; in water, currents can carry it. The difference in habitat explains the difference in habit.
evidence: for we know of no means, analogous to the action of insects and of the wind in the case of plants, by which an occasional cross could be effected with terrestrial animals without the concurrence of two individuals

questions.prompt: How does Darwin state his conclusion, and how confident is it? Count his qualifications.
facilitatorNotes: “Strongly inclined to suspect,” “many cases of difficulty,” “as I suspect”: the conclusion is graded, certain for some organisms and only probable for all. Readers can judge whether the hedging is a weakness or a model of stating a claim at the strength the evidence allows.
evidence: I am strongly inclined to suspect
in none, as I suspect, can self-fertilisation go on for perpetuity

readings.title: Origin of Species: Numbers, time and crossing (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Track how one factor, intercrossing, both hinders and helps.
readings.focus: What makes natural selection faster or slower: numbers, time and crossing.
readings.context: In Chapter IV Darwin has described natural selection and sexual selection and argued that an occasional cross between individuals is a law of nature. Now he asks what conditions help or hinder selection. The polity or economy of nature is the system of places that species fill; methodical selection is a breeder’s deliberate choice, unconscious selection the slow effect of everyone keeping their best animals; stations are the particular sites a species frequents.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Natural Selection,” from “Circumstances favourable to Natural Selection” to the uniforming effect of crosses; opens “_Circumstances favourable to Natural Selection_.—This is an extremely intricate subject.…”; closes “…offspring, solely by natural selection preserving the same favourable variations.”.

questions.prompt: Nature grants “vast periods of time,” Darwin says, but “not an indefinite period.” Why not?
facilitatorNotes: All beings are striving to seize places, so a species that is not improved as fast as its competitors “will soon be exterminated.” Time is limited by the pace of rivals, not by the age of the earth.
evidence: she does not grant an indefinite period
it will soon be exterminated

questions.prompt: Why does free crossing stop a breeder’s methodical selection but not the “unconscious” selection Darwin compares with nature?
facilitatorNotes: A breeder aiming at a definite object loses his work if his animals cross freely. But when many people share a rough standard and all keep their best animals, improvement follows even with much crossing. In a confined area nature acts like the many breeders, preserving all individuals that vary “in the right direction.”
evidence: free intercrossing will wholly stop his work
notwithstanding a large amount of crossing with inferior animals

questions.prompt: Which animals does Darwin expect crossing to affect most, and what prediction about birds follows?
facilitatorNotes: Those that pair for each birth, wander widely and breed slowly; so in birds, varieties should be confined to separated countries, which he believes to be so. Animals that stay put and breed fast can form a local variety quickly. The argument produces a checkable prediction.
evidence: The intercrossing will most affect those animals which unite for each birth, which wander much, and which do not breed at a very quick rate.
varieties will generally be confined to separated countries

questions.prompt: Crossing can slow the formation of new varieties, yet Darwin says it “plays a very important part” in keeping a species true. How can one process do both?
facilitatorNotes: Crossing blends local differences, so it resists divergence, but by blending it also keeps a species uniform; and crossed offspring gain vigour and fertility, so they survive better. The same mixing that holds back change preserves the type.
evidence: Intercrossing plays a very important part in nature in keeping the individuals of the same species, or of the same variety, true and uniform in character.

readings.title: Origin of Species: Islands, continents and living fossils (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Weigh two hypotheses when the decisive comparison cannot be made.
readings.focus: Whether new species form best on isolated islands or on large continents, and why some ancient forms survive.
readings.context: Darwin is weighing the conditions that favour natural selection: large numbers, time and limited crossing. Now he asks whether new species form best in small isolated areas, such as oceanic islands, or on large continents. Endemic species occur in one place only; oscillations of level are the rise and fall of land; Madeira is an Atlantic island; the Ornithorhynchus is the platypus and Lepidosiren the South American lungfish; Ganoid fishes are an ancient group that includes sturgeons and gars.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Natural Selection,” from the effects of isolation to the forms surviving in fresh water; opens “Isolation, also, is an important element in the process of natural selection. In a…”; closes “…inhabited a confined area, and from having thus been exposed to less severe competition.”.

questions.prompt: List the ways Darwin says isolation helps natural selection, and the way it hurts.
facilitatorNotes: It gives uniform conditions, so all individuals are modified alike; it prevents crossing with neighbours living under other conditions; above all it keeps out better-adapted immigrants, leaving new places for the old inhabitants; and it gives time. But a very small area supports few individuals, and fewness means fewer favourable variations.
evidence: isolation probably acts more efficiently in checking the immigration of better adapted organisms
fewness of individuals will greatly retard the production of new species

questions.prompt: Oceanic islands have many endemic species. Why does Darwin refuse to conclude that islands are the best places for new species?
facilitatorNotes: The fair test would compare island and continent “within equal times,” and that cannot be done. Darwin shows a scientist declining a tempting inference because the comparison is uncontrolled.
evidence: we ought to make the comparison within equal times; and this we are incapable of doing

questions.prompt: On balance Darwin favours large areas. What reasons does he give?
facilitatorNotes: More individuals, so more favourable variations; more species, so more complex conditions and harder competition; room for improved forms to spread; and past breaks in the land that gave some benefits of isolation anyway. Forms that win on a continent have beaten many rivals and spread most widely.
evidence: on the whole I am inclined to believe that largeness of area is of more importance
the new forms produced on large areas, which already have been victorious over many competitors, will be those that will spread most widely

questions.prompt: Darwin calls the platypus and the lungfish “living fossils.” What does he mean, and how does his explanation fit his argument?
facilitatorNotes: They are odd forms that link groups now far apart, like fossils, yet still alive. Fresh water is a small, broken area where competition is weaker, so old forms were exterminated more slowly. The coinage follows directly from his claim that area governs the severity of competition.
evidence: These anomalous forms may almost be called living fossils
from having thus been exposed to less severe competition

readings.title: Origin of Species: Slowness and extinction (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Lay out the premises of an argument that something “inevitably follows.”
readings.focus: Darwin admits selection is slow, and argues that extinction is its necessary partner.
readings.context: Darwin has weighed numbers, crossing, isolation and the size of an area as conditions for natural selection, and has argued that large areas produce the most successful new forms. Here he sums up, concedes that selection is slow, and introduces extinction, which he treats more fully in his chapters on geology. Subsidence and elevation are the sinking and rising of land; incipient species are species in the making; long-horns and short-horns are breeds of cattle.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Natural Selection,” from the summary of favourable circumstances to the section on extinction; opens “To sum up the circumstances favourable and unfavourable to natural selection, as far as…”; closes “…(I quote the words of an agricultural writer) “as if by some murderous pestilence.””.

questions.prompt: Darwin’s summary imagines a continent that sinks into islands and later rises again. Trace the stages and what each contributes.
facilitatorNotes: As a continent it holds many individuals in severe competition; as islands, crossing and immigration are checked and varieties have time to improve; rejoined, the improved forms spread, the less improved die out, and selection starts again. The imagined history combines the benefits of large areas and of isolation.
evidence: When converted by subsidence into large separate islands
When, by renewed elevation, the islands shall be re-converted into a continental area, there will again be severe competition

questions.prompt: “That natural selection will always act with extreme slowness, I fully admit.” Why does Darwin concede this so readily, and how does he turn it to his advantage?
facilitatorNotes: Slowness is what geology shows of the rate at which living things have changed, so the concession becomes evidence for him. He then argues from the breeder: if “feeble man” achieves so much quickly, nature with vast time has no limit. Readers can ask whether “no limit” goes beyond what the analogy supports.
evidence: this very slow, intermittent action of natural selection accords perfectly well with what geology tells us
if feeble man can do much by his powers of artificial selection, I can see no limit to the amount of change

questions.prompt: Follow the argument that many species “inevitably must become extinct.” On what premises does it rest, and where does Darwin qualify it?
facilitatorNotes: Every area is fully stocked; favoured forms increase, so others decrease; rarity precedes extinction; new forms keep appearing while the number of species has not grown without limit. Then he admits that no region may yet be fully stocked: plants naturalised at the Cape of Good Hope drove out no natives. The conclusion is strong; the qualification is honest.
evidence: Rarity, as geology tells us, is the precursor to extinction.
Probably no region is as yet fully stocked

questions.prompt: Why does each new variety “press hardest on its nearest kindred”? What does the quotation about Yorkshire cattle add?
facilitatorNotes: Closest relatives share structure, constitution and habits, so they compete most severely, as Chapter III argued. The quoted agricultural writer, describing breeds swept away “as if by some murderous pestilence,” gives a vivid, practical witness from domestic history rather than theory.
evidence: will generally press hardest on its nearest kindred, and tend to exterminate them
as if by some murderous pestilence.

readings.title: Origin of Species: Not chance, but ignorance (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice how Darwin separates what he can conclude from what he admits he does not know.
readings.focus: What causes variation: chance, climate, or the disturbed reproductive system of the parents.
readings.context: Chapter IV argued that natural selection preserves favourable variations; Chapter V asks where variations come from. Darwin wrote before anyone understood how heredity works. A monstrosity is a large deviation of structure; a “sporting” plant puts out a shoot unlike the rest of the plant; an ovule is the part that becomes a seed; furriers deal in furs.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Laws of Variation,” from the opening on “chance” to the indirect action of the conditions of life; opens “I have hitherto sometimes spoken as if the variations—so common and multiform in organic…”; closes “…variations, however slight, until they become plainly developed and appreciable by us.”.

questions.prompt: Darwin calls “chance” “a wholly incorrect expression.” Why has he used it, and what does he believe instead?
facilitatorNotes: It was a plain way of admitting ignorance of each variation’s cause. He believes every deviation has a cause, chiefly the conditions of life acting on the parents’ reproductive system, even when we cannot name it.
evidence: it serves to acknowledge plainly our ignorance of the cause of each particular variation
we may feel sure that there must be some cause for each deviation of structure, however slight

questions.prompt: What evidence leads him to connect variation with the conditions of life?
facilitatorNotes: Domestic and cultivated forms vary far more, and produce more monstrosities, than wild ones; he has also noted in Chapter I that the reproductive system is sensitive to changed conditions. The inference runs from a correlation (more change of conditions, more variation) to a cause.
evidence: the much greater variability, as well as the greater frequency of monstrosities, under domestication or cultivation, than under nature

questions.prompt: Darwin calls the direct effect of climate “extremely small,” yet paragraph 189 uses facts about colour and fleshy leaves to support his theory. How?
facilitatorNotes: Varieties that range into another species’ zone take on a little of its character, which fits his view that species are only well-marked varieties. A believer in separate creation must explain the same pattern twice: one shell created bright for a warm sea, another made bright by variation. Darwin’s single explanation is simpler.
evidence: accords with our view that species of all kinds are only well-marked and permanent varieties
He who believes in the creation of each species, will have to say

questions.prompt: Why can no one tell how much of an animal’s thicker fur in a cold climate is due to selection and how much to the climate itself? What evidence would separate the two?
facilitatorNotes: Both causes push in the same direction, so the result cannot show which acted. One would need a comparison that holds one cause constant, such as the same stock in a cold climate without selection, which nature does not supply. Darwin concludes that conditions act mostly “indirectly,” by inducing variability.
evidence: who can tell how much of this difference may be due to the warmest-clad individuals having been favoured
Such facts show how indirectly the conditions of life must act.

readings.title: Origin of Species: Wingless beetles of Madeira (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Weigh two possible causes of the same result and follow how Darwin decides between them.
readings.focus: Flightless birds, dung beetles without feet, and wingless beetles: disuse or natural selection?
readings.context: Darwin accepted that organs strengthened by use or weakened by disuse pass those changes to offspring; biologists today do not accept that such changes are inherited, so read for how he weighs this cause against natural selection. Tarsi are an insect’s feet; coleoptera are beetles and lepidoptera butterflies and moths; Madeira and the nearby Dezertas are Atlantic islands; endemic means found nowhere else.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Laws of Variation,” “Effects of Use and Disuse,” from flightless birds to the insects of Madeira; opens “_Effects of Use and Disuse_.—From the facts alluded to in the first chapter, I think…”; closes “…for the bad swimmers if they had not been able to swim at all and had stuck to the wreck.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin reject inherited mutilation as the reason Ateuchus has no front feet? What does he propose instead?
facilitatorNotes: There is no good evidence that mutilations are inherited. Because the feet break off early in life and so are little used, he credits “the long-continued effects of disuse.” A modern reader can note that this, too, assumes an inheritance biology no longer accepts.
evidence: There is not sufficient evidence to induce us to believe that mutilations are ever inherited
by the long-continued effects of disuse in their progenitors

questions.prompt: List the facts that make Darwin credit natural selection, more than disuse, for Madeira’s wingless beetles.
facilitatorNotes: Beetles are often blown out to sea; Madeira beetles hide until the wind drops; wingless ones are commoner on the exposed Dezertas; groups that must fly are almost absent. Over generations, the beetle that flew least was likeliest to survive.
evidence: that the proportion of wingless beetles is larger on the exposed Dezertas than in Madeira itself
will have had the best chance of surviving from not being blown out to sea

questions.prompt: Flower-feeding insects on Madeira have larger wings, not smaller. Why does this not contradict the theory?
facilitatorNotes: Selection favours whichever saves more individuals: for insects that must fly to feed, stronger wings that win against the wind. The same pressure, the wind, pushes different insects in opposite directions.
evidence: This is quite compatible with the action of natural selection.
whether a greater number of individuals were saved by successfully battling with the winds

questions.prompt: Explain the comparison with shipwrecked mariners. Is it a good analogy?
facilitatorNotes: Good swimmers would gain by swimming further, poor swimmers by not trying and staying with the wreck: the middle course is worst. It clarifies why selection can drive wings to either extreme. Its limit is that mariners choose, while beetles do not; the “choice” is made by survival over many generations.
evidence: it would have been better for the good swimmers if they had been able to swim still further
had stuck to the wreck

readings.title: Origin of Species: Blind animals of the caves (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow an argument that tests two explanations, separate creation and descent, against the same facts.
readings.focus: Why blind cave animals resemble their neighbours outside the caves, not each other.
readings.context: Darwin has been explaining some features by use and disuse, assuming (as biologists today do not) that changes from disuse are inherited. Styria is a region of Austria. The nictitating membrane is a third eyelid; palpi are feelers near an insect’s mouth; Proteus is a blind cave animal of Europe; Agassiz was a Swiss-American naturalist.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Laws of Variation,” “Effects of Use and Disuse,” from the eyes of moles to the blind animals of the caves; opens “The eyes of moles and of some burrowing rodents are rudimentary in size, and in some…”; closes “…to which the inhabitants of these dark abodes will probably have been exposed.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Darwin credit natural selection with helping to reduce the mole’s eyes, but the loss of eyes in cave animals “wholly to disuse”?
facilitatorNotes: For burrowers, eyes can be harmful (inflammation), so smaller, covered eyes could be an advantage that selection preserves. In total darkness he cannot see how eyes could harm their owner, so he finds no advantage for selection to act on. Today biologists would explain cave blindness without inherited disuse, but the distinction he draws is careful.
evidence: As frequent inflammation of the eyes must be injurious to any animal
I attribute their loss wholly to disuse

questions.prompt: “The stand for the telescope is there, though the telescope with its glasses has been lost.” What does this image say about the crab’s eye-stalk?
facilitatorNotes: A structure that remains after its function is gone is evidence of history: the crab’s ancestors had eyes. The comparison makes a rudimentary part look like a clue left behind.
evidence: the stand for the telescope is there, though the telescope with its glasses has been lost

questions.prompt: What would separate creation predict about the blind animals of American and European caves, and what is actually found?
facilitatorNotes: Similar conditions should produce similar creatures, so the cave faunas of the two continents should be closely alike. Instead each is allied to the animals of its own continent, as descent predicts if animals gradually moved into the caves from outside.
evidence: close similarity in their organisation and affinities might have been expected
the cave-insects of the two continents are not more closely allied than might have been anticipated

questions.prompt: Why is Darwin “only surprised that more wrecks of ancient life have not been preserved” in caves?
facilitatorNotes: Competition is less severe in the dark, so old forms could survive there longer than outside, like the anomalous forms Chapter IV found on islands and in fresh water. “Wrecks” makes them survivors of a lost world.
evidence: I am only surprised that more wrecks of ancient life have not been preserved
owing to the less severe competition

readings.title: Origin of Species: Acclimatisation (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Sort Darwin’s evidence into what is observed, what is inferred, and what he says has never been tested.
readings.focus: Whether species can become fitted to new climates, and how habit and selection might share the work.
readings.context: Darwin believes all species of a genus descend from one parent, though one genus often has species in very hot and very cold countries. Acclimatisation is becoming fitted to a new climate. Joseph Hooker was a botanist who collected plants in the Himalaya; Ceylon is now Sri Lanka. “Uncivilised man” is a period phrase for early peoples.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Laws of Variation,” “Acclimatisation,” the whole section; opens “_Acclimatisation_.—Habit is hereditary with plants, as in the period of flowering, in the…”; closes “…with, and sometimes overmastered by, the natural selection of innate differences.”.
