questions.prompt: Why does Darwin’s theory require that acclimatisation be “readily effected”?
facilitatorNotes: If species of one genus living in hot and cold countries share one parent, their ancestors must have adapted to new climates as they spread. A theory of common descent that could not explain this would fail.
evidence: as I believe that all the species of the same genus have descended from a single parent
acclimatisation must be readily effected during long-continued descent

questions.prompt: What reasons does Darwin give for thinking that adaptation to climate “is often overrated”?
facilitatorNotes: We cannot predict whether an imported plant will survive; many animals and plants from warmer countries thrive here; ranges are limited by competitors as much as by climate; domestic animals, rats and mice live almost everywhere; and extinct elephants and rhinoceroses endured glacial cold.
evidence: our frequent inability to predict whether or not an imported plant will endure our climate
species in a state of nature are limited in their ranges by the competition of other organic beings

questions.prompt: How does Darwin use American fruit-tree catalogues against the idea that acclimatisation is only habit?
facilitatorNotes: Some varieties are recommended for northern states and others for southern; since most are recent, the difference cannot come from long habit and must be innate, the kind of difference natural selection can work on.
evidence: as most of these varieties are of recent origin, they cannot owe their constitutional differences to habit

questions.prompt: Describe the kidney-bean experiment Darwin proposes. Why does he say it “cannot be said to have been even tried”?
facilitatorNotes: Sow beans early enough for frost to kill most, save seed from the survivors, prevent crosses, and repeat for twenty generations: selection for hardiness. Merely noting that beans stay tender proves nothing without selection, and the Jerusalem artichoke, never grown from seed, produces no new varieties to select from. The passage is a lesson in designing a fair test.
evidence: the experiment cannot be said to have been even tried
which is never propagated by seed, and of which consequently new varieties have not been produced

readings.title: Origin of Species: Correlation of growth (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Hold on to an idea Darwin calls “most imperfectly understood” and judge how much his examples can show.
readings.focus: Parts that vary together, and structures that may be of no use at all.
readings.context: Darwin has argued that natural selection keeps useful variations. Here he considers changes that come along with others because the body grows as one connected whole. Homologous parts share the same basic origin, such as front and hind legs; a corolla is a flower’s ring of petals; ray florets are the outer, petal-like flowers of a daisy head; an umbel is a flower cluster like that of parsley; viscera are internal organs; systematists classify living things.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Laws of Variation,” “Correlation of Growth,” from its definition to the seeds of the Umbelliferæ; opens “_Correlation of Growth_.—I mean by this expression that the whole organisation is so tied…”; closes “…growth, and without being, as far as we can see, of the slightest service to the species.”.

questions.prompt: Define “correlation of growth” in your own words, using one of Darwin’s examples.
facilitatorNotes: Because the organism is “tied together” as it grows, a change in one part brings changes in others: changes selected for a larva affect the adult; the right and left sides, or front and hind legs, vary together.
evidence: the whole organisation is so tied together during its growth and development
we see this in the right and left sides of the body varying in the same manner

questions.prompt: Darwin lists strange pairings, such as blue eyes and deafness in cats. What do these examples show, and what do they not show?
facilitatorNotes: They show that traits can be linked “without our being able to assign any reason.” They do not show the mechanism; he admits the bond is “very frequently quite obscure.” Their value is to warn that a trait may be present because of its link to another, not for its own use.
evidence: The nature of the bond of correlation is very frequently quite obscure.
without our being able to assign any reason

questions.prompt: Follow Darwin’s reasoning about the inner and outer flowers. Which explanations does he test, and why does he set them aside?
facilitatorNotes: Pressure: but the flowers do not differ most in the densest heads. Ray petals drawing nourishment from other parts: but some seeds differ without any difference in the corolla. He leaves a possible difference in “the flow of nutriment,” and allows Sprengel’s idea that ray florets attract insects, which selection could favour.
evidence: it is by no means, as Dr. Hooker informs me, in species with the densest heads that the inner and outer flowers most frequently differ
but in some Compositæ there is a difference in the seeds of the outer and inner florets without any difference in the corolla

questions.prompt: The section ends by saying that structures valued by classifiers “may be wholly due to unknown laws of correlated growth.” Why is this an important admission for a theory of natural selection?
facilitatorNotes: It concedes that not every feature is adaptive and that selection is not the only source of form, which guards the theory against claiming too much. It also warns classifiers that a feature used to divide groups may be a useless side effect. Some readers will see a weakness; others the honesty that makes the rest more credible.
evidence: may be wholly due to unknown laws of correlated growth, and without being, as far as we can see, of the slightest service to the species
it seems impossible that they can be in any way advantageous to the plant

readings.title: Origin of Species: The variable extraordinary part (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Track a rule, its limits, an analogy from breeding and its application to nature, and see where each step depends on the theory.
readings.focus: Why the most remarkable part of a species tends to be its most variable.
readings.context: Darwin is setting out such “laws of variation” as he can make out. Cirripedes are barnacles, which Darwin had studied for years; opercular valves are the plates that close a barnacle’s shell. Secondary sexual characters belong to one sex without being part of reproduction itself. Fanciers breed pigeons for show; tumblers, carriers, fantails and pouters are breeds, and a wattle is a fleshy growth on the head. A geological period is one of the long divisions of the earth’s history.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Laws of Variation,” from the rule that a part developed in an extraordinary degree is highly variable to its explanation in nature; opens “_A part developed in any species in an extraordinary degree or manner, in comparison with…”; closes “…continued rejection of those tending to revert to a former and less modified condition.”.

questions.prompt: State the rule in your own words. Why does it not apply to the bat’s wing?
facilitatorNotes: A part developed unusually compared with the same part in closely allied species tends to vary a great deal. The bat’s wing is abnormal among mammals, but every bat has one, so the comparison with close relatives shows nothing unusual.
evidence: unless it be unusually developed in comparison with the same part in closely allied species
because there is a whole group of bats having wings

questions.prompt: Darwin cannot give “the long array of facts” and admits the rule may fail for plants. How should a reader weigh a claim offered on these terms?
facilitatorNotes: He offers a “conviction,” one striking example (the barnacle Pyrgoma) and birds, names “causes of error,” and admits the plant problem. A fair reader treats it as a provisional rule awaiting the full evidence, and may count the admissions in its favour.
evidence: I can only state my conviction that it is a rule of high generality.
this would seriously have shaken my belief in its truth

questions.prompt: What happens to a breed’s “points” while fanciers are actively selecting them? How does this give Darwin his analogy?
facilitatorNotes: The points under rapid selection vary the most: there is a “constant struggle” between reversion and fresh variability on one side and steady selection on the other, which selection wins in the long run. Nature, he argues, works the same way.
evidence: those points, which at the present time are undergoing rapid change by continued selection, are also eminently liable to variation
There may be truly said to be a constant struggle going on

questions.prompt: How does descent with modification explain the rule in nature, and why does separate creation explain nothing?
facilitatorNotes: An extraordinary part has been greatly modified since the species branched off, recently in geological terms, so its variability has not yet been fixed; an organ like the bat’s wing, inherited for an immense time, has become constant. On separate creation there is no reason an important organ should vary more than others.
evidence: On the view that each species has been independently created, with all its parts as we now see them, I can see no explanation.
It is only in those cases in which the modification has been comparatively recent and extraordinarily great

readings.title: Origin of Species: Stripes on horses (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Gather many small observations into one hypothesis, then test it against a rival hypothesis and against separate creation.
readings.focus: Stripes that reappear in asses, horses and hybrids, and what they suggest about a striped common ancestor.
readings.context: Darwin has argued that related species vary in similar ways and that a variety may revert to the character of a remote ancestor, as the bars of the wild blue rock-pigeon reappear when pigeon breeds are crossed. The horse-genus includes horses, asses, zebras and the hemionus, an Asian wild ass; the quagga, a South African zebra striped only on the front of its body, was hunted to extinction later in the century. Dun is a sandy or greyish-brown coat; a foal is a young horse; the hock is a joint of the hind leg. Cosmogonists are theorists of the world’s origin.
readings.contentNote: Historical scientific prose from 1859. Darwin’s explanatory hypotheses and terminology are presented for analysis of his reasoning, not as a current biology reference.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “Laws of Variation,” the case of stripes in the horse-genus, from the ass to the “mockery and deception” of separate creation; opens “I will, however, give one curious and complex case, not indeed as affecting any important…”; closes “…but had been created in stone so as to mock the shells now living on the sea-shore.”.

questions.prompt: List three kinds of evidence Darwin collects for stripes in the horse-genus.
facilitatorNotes: Variation within species (leg bars in asses; spinal, shoulder and leg stripes in horses, especially duns); age (stripes plainest in foals); and hybrids between species, which are often more striped than either parent. He adds geographic range, from Britain to China.
evidence: The stripes are plainest in the foal
I have collected cases of leg and shoulder stripes in horses of very different breeds, in various countries from Britain to Eastern China

questions.prompt: How does Darwin answer Colonel Hamilton Smith’s theory that striped horses inherit their stripes from crosses with a striped wild dun species?
facilitatorNotes: He will not apply it to breeds so distinct and distant as Belgian cart-horses, Welsh ponies and Kattywar horses. The hybrid evidence also tells against it: crosses between species that lack stripes produce striped offspring.
evidence: But I am not at all satisfied with this theory
breeds so distinct as the heavy Belgian cart-horse, Welch ponies, cobs, the lanky Kattywar race

questions.prompt: Why did a hybrid’s face-stripes lead Darwin to write to Colonel Poole? What does this show about his method?
facilitatorNotes: Convinced that no stripe appears by accident, he predicted that face-stripes should also occur in the most striped horse breed, asked, and was told yes. It is a small, tested prediction, the strongest kind of evidence in the passage.
evidence: I was so convinced that not even a stripe of colour appears from what would commonly be called an accident
and was, as we have seen, answered in the affirmative

questions.prompt: Darwin says the alternative view “makes the works of God a mere mockery and deception.” Explain the argument. Is it scientific, theological, or both?
facilitatorNotes: On separate creation, each species would have been made with a tendency to imitate the stripes of other species, a deceptive design like fossils created in stone. Scientifically he prefers a real cause (descent) to “an unreal, or at least … an unknown” one; theologically he appeals to readers who believe God does not deceive. Students may argue it is both, aimed at a religious audience.
evidence: to reject a real for an unreal, or at least for an unknown, cause
that fossil shells had never lived, but had been created in stone so as to mock the shells now living on the sea-shore
